name: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso)

lead: Mirvaso is a 0.33% brimonidine tartrate gel, approved by the FDA in 2013 for the facial redness of rosacea, that visibly reduces redness within hours of application. It was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition.

Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions. It activates receptors in the skin's blood vessels, causing them to constrict so less blood shows at the surface. Rosacea overviews place the peak effect at roughly 3 to 6 hours after application, and the effect is temporary.

paras: People apply it to the face as a daily gel under a prescription, often timed before events or work since the effect peaks hours after application. It is used alongside other rosacea care such as sunscreen and anti-inflammatory creams.

Reported adverse effects include flushing or redness worse than baseline, allergic contact dermatitis, severe rebound erythema in case reports, and one reported case of symptomatic bradycardia. It is prescription-only in many countries.

angle.text: Brimonidine gel narrows facial blood vessels so less blood shows near the surface, visibly reducing rosacea redness within hours. The effect is temporary, and the product has had FDA approval for this use since 2013. Rebound redness has been reported in some users.

lead: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso, brimonidine tartrate 0.33%) was approved by the US FDA in 2013 for facial erythema of rosacea and was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition [1][2]. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, first patented in 1972 and in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions [1].

For appearance, the point is temporary reduction of visible facial redness. Brimonidine narrows the small blood vessels of the skin, so a flushed or persistently red face looks more even for several hours after a single application. It does not treat the underlying condition; Wikipedia's rosacea article says medications often give a temporary remission of redness that usually returns when treatment stops.[3]

Rosacea overviews describe brimonidine as constricting vessels to reduce redness, with a peak effect 3 to 6 hours after application [1]. A review of facial erythema in rosacea places the redness in the context of immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction [4].
Published case reports describe adverse reactions including allergic contact dermatitis [5][6], rebound erythema [7][8] and a case of symptomatic bradycardia [9].
infobox: Peak effect about 3 to 6 hours after application[1]

paras: Mirvaso is a clear gel containing 0.33% brimonidine tartrate, applied to the face once daily for persistent redness in adults with rosacea.[1][2] Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist; the same molecule is used in eye drops for glaucoma and, at lower concentrations, in drops sold for eye redness.[1]

Rosacea is a common, chronic facial skin condition with persistent redness, flushing, visible vessels and sometimes bumps. Wikipedia reports estimates of 1 to 10% of people affected, more often fair-skinned people, with triggers that include sunlight, temperature extremes, alcohol, hot drinks, spicy foods, exercise and stress.[3] Persistent facial redness was long considered difficult to treat directly, and brimonidine was described at launch as targeting it specifically.[2][10]

The gel is indicated for persistent facial redness of rosacea in adults [8][1]. The same ingredient appears in ophthalmic products for glaucoma and ocular redness, some available over the counter in the US [1].

A 2014 Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin appraisal and a SkinMed product summary reviewed the product at launch [2][10]. A small imaging study used optical coherence tomography to monitor treatment response [11]. Registered post-marketing studies include open-label studies of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey [12][13][14]; results are not summarised here. Because the effect is a vessel constriction, rosacea references describe it as reducing redness during the hours of effect rather than altering the disease [1].

A multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study of brimonidine gel 0.33% reported rapid improvement in patient-reported outcomes of facial erythema.[15] Medical Letter reviews in 2013 and 2024 summarise brimonidine among the topical options for rosacea redness, alongside oxymetazoline and treatments for the bumps and pimples of rosacea.[16][17] Laser and intense pulsed light, which target visible vessels rather than general flushing, are a separate approach described in encyclopaedic summaries.[3]

Commonly reported adverse events include redness or flushing worse than baseline, most often with the first application [8]. Case reports describe a paradoxical erythema reaction with long-term use [8], severe rebound erythema labelled dermatitis medicamentosa [7], and allergic contact dermatitis, including sensitisation in two cases [5][6]. A 2024 case report described symptomatic bradycardia after use [9]. Systemic effects of brimonidine in other forms include low blood pressure and dry mouth [1].
Brimonidine constricts blood vessels through alpha-2 adrenergic activation, which in the skin reduces redness [1].

Rosacea reviews describe the redness as arising from immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction, with dilated cutaneous vessels; brimonidine acts on the vessel wall rather than on those upstream processes.[4][1] Wikipedia lists the peak improvement at three to six hours after application.[3] Oxymetazoline cream, a related alpha-agonist approved later, is covered in its own entry.[18]

Human studies include open-label post-marketing trials in rosacea [12][13], a utilisation study [14] and a small imaging study [11]. Studies in other conditions (hand-foot syndrome, flushing in aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency) are registered but concern other uses [19][20].

The pivotal-type evidence includes the randomised, vehicle-controlled JEADV study of patient-reported outcomes.[15] A randomised trial in Asian individuals tested topical brimonidine against alcohol-induced facial flushing, a use outside rosacea.[21] Registered post-marketing studies of Mirvaso include open-label trials of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey.[12][13][14]
The gel is mentioned in skincare circles as an option for temporary redness before events, typically alongside discussion of rebound redness reports.

Users who mention it describe it as a short-lived corrector, applied before a photo or event, in the same conversation as green-tinted concealer, sunscreen and trigger avoidance. Reports of rebound redness are part of how the product is discussed, and the case-report literature describes the same reaction.[8][7]

The gel was approved by the US FDA in 2013 and is a prescription product in many countries, while brimonidine eye drops for redness are sold over the counter in some markets.[1] Case reports of allergic reactions, paradoxical redness, severe rebound and bradycardia are the basis for the cautions discussed in clinical reviews.[5][8][6][7][9]

timeline.event: FDA approves Mirvaso gel 0.33% for facial erythema of rosacea.[1]
